theme: I am the LORD your God, if only my people would listen
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 81. It is a festival psalm in which God himself speaks and pleads with his people. Notice how it moves from joyful praise to a wistful “if only.”
settingTheScene: Psalm 81 is a psalm of Asaph, to be sung at a festival, probably the Feast of Tabernacles or Passover, as it refers to the new moon and the full moon. The people are called to celebrate. Then, in verse 5, the voice shifts, and God himself speaks. The psalm pairs with Psalm 80: there the people asked God to restore them, and here God asks them why they will not listen.
observation: “Sing aloud to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob!” (v. 1).
“I relieved your shoulder of the burden; your hands were freed from the basket” (v. 6).
“In distress you called, and I delivered you” (v. 7).
“Hear, O my people, while I admonish you! O Israel, if you would but listen to me!” (v. 8).
“There shall be no strange god among you; you shall not bow down to a foreign god” (v. 9).
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (v. 10).
“But my people did not listen to my voice; Israel would not submit to me” (v. 11).
“Oh, that my people would listen to me, that Israel would walk in my ways! … I would feed you with the finest of the wheat, and with honey from the rock I would satisfy you” (vv. 13, 16).
interpretation:
The first part of the psalm is exuberant. Musical instruments are named: tambourine, lyre, harp, trumpet. The people are told to celebrate because it is a statute for Israel. Worship is an obligation, and it is also a delight.

Then God speaks, and the voice is full of pathos. He reminds them of the exodus: he relieved their shoulders of the burden, freed their hands from the baskets of brick-making, and answered them in the thunder. He tested them at the waters of Meribah. The history is in the background of everything that follows.

God’s central appeal is verse 8: “Hear, O my people.” It echoes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6. The first commandment follows: no strange god among you. And then a promise that is also an invitation: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” Like a baby bird with its beak open, the people are invited to depend on their provider. God is not reluctant. He has more to give than they dare ask.

The sad part comes in verse 11. “But my people did not listen to my voice.” So God “gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.” Sometimes the worst judgment is to be left to what we want.

The psalm ends with God’s wistful “if only.” If they would listen, if they would walk in his ways, he would subdue their enemies and feed them with the finest wheat and honey from the rock. This is God’s heart. He does not delight in judgment. He longs for his people to listen and to receive his blessings.
connection: Jesus said, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28), the same relief of burdens. John 6:35 says he is the bread of life, the finest wheat. 1 Corinthians 10:4 says that the rock in the wilderness was Christ, from whom flowed the water, and in Psalm 81 the honey. Luke 13:34 echoes the divine longing: “How often would I have gathered your children… and you would not!” Revelation 3:20 shows Christ knocking at the door.
application:
Ask where God is saying “if only you would listen” to you. What is he asking that you have not done?

Open your mouth wide. Bring a large request to God this week, a need for yourself or for others.

Thank God for the burdens he has lifted from your shoulders.
prayerPrompts: Shout to God for his strength, and tell him why.
Confess where you have not listened to his voice.
Ask him to open your ears.
